etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin stimulus (“goad, prick”).

definitions.definition: An external phenomenon that has an influence on a system, by triggering or modifying an internal phenomenon; for example, a spur or incentive that drives a person to take action or change behaviour.

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XV, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume II, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 174:
quote.text: From the beginning of the show to the end, vanity is the sole stimulus and reward of action—vanity, that never looks beyond the present.

quote.citation: 2012 November 7, Matt Bai, “Winning a Second Term, Obama Will Confront Familiar Headwinds”, in New York Times‎[1]:
quote.text: Democrats, meanwhile, point out that Republicans seem to have made a conscious decision, beginning with the stimulus, to oppose anything the president put forward, dooming any chance of renewed cooperation between the parties.

definitions.definition: (physiology, psychology, medicine) Something external that elicits or influences a physiological or psychological activity or response, or that affects any of the sensory apparatuses.

quote.citation: 2002, Kim Burchiel, Surgical Management of Pain, Thieme, →ISBN, page 44:
quote.text: Even light nonpainful stimuli can provoke or exacerbate spontaneous pain; this is not limited to tactile, thermal, or vibratory stimuli, because auditory, visual, olfactory, and visceral stimuli also may be problematic.

definitions.definition: (botany, entomology) A stinging part on the body of a plant or insect.

quote.citation: 1789, Erasmus Darwin, The Loves of the Plants, J. Johnson, page 15:
quote.text: Many plants, like many animals, are furnished with arms for their protection; these are either aculei, prickles  […] ; or stimuli, stings, as in the nettles, which are armed with a venomous fluid for the annoyance of naked animals.
